title: Sustainable Alternative Solutions for Unpaved Forest Roads: Combining Aggregate, Exhausted Sands and Geogrids
abstract: Abstract Traditionally, road construction depends on natural, virgin aggregates, which are becoming scarcer, creating a need for alternative and sustainable replacements. Wastes and industrial byproducts show potential for incorporation in pavement structures, preventing landfill disposal and reducing reliability on natural resources, while ensuring adequate performance. Geosynthetics provide increased strength and durability, offering cost-effective and sustainable solutions for roads. This paper assesses benefits of combining an aggregate with exhausted sands and geogrids for unpaved forest roads. It includes: geotechnical characterisation of two exhausted sands, including their shear behaviour and load-bearing response; design of an unpaved forest road section for different foundation scenarios, considering different solutions for the base layer using unbound materials (aggregate, exhausted sands), without and with geogrid reinforcement; and a cost analysis of solutions designed for a particular case study. The physical and geotechnical characterisation of the exhausted sands demonstrates that their geotechnical application was viable, and that there were no statistical differences between the two exhausted sands. All the solutions were optimised by the inclusion of geogrids, which result in a significant reduction in the height of the base layer. Results also showed that, for the case study considered, using these materials over traditional aggregates is more cost-effective when the transport distances for exhausted sands supply do not surpass 200 km. Above this distance, if traditional aggregates are obtained at a shorter distance, profitability is reversed. In all solutions the use of geogrid further enhances cost savings in acquisition and transport.
journal: International Journal of Geosynthetics and Ground Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Unpaved forest roads are a crucial component of rural and forest transport networks, ensuring access for rural communities, agricultural activities, forestry operations, firefighting and leisure. These facilities have some design and maintenance challenges due to heavy seasonal traffic associated with agricultural and forest activities, high moisture variability, and remote locations. Unpaved forest road construction has traditionally relied on the use of high-quality natural aggregates, valued for their mechanical stability and performance under traffic loading. However, these resources are becoming scarcer in nature [ 1 ] and, due to environmental concerns regarding the extraction process from quarries, alternative solutions are emerging as sustainable replacements [ 2 ].

One viable strategy is to minimize the height of the aggregate layers, without compromising performance, by using geosynthetics [ 3 ]. Thus, given the fact that good-quality aggregates represent a major cost component, accounting for 40–80% of total construction expenses [ 4 ], materials such as geosynthetics can provide a cost-effective and sustainable solution by enabling the reduction of base layer thickness and facilitating increased strength and durability [ 3 ,  5 ]. Geogrids have been successfully applied in roadways in general [ 6 ,  7 ] and unpaved roads, in particular [ 8 ,  9 ]. By promoting an efficient stress distribution across pavement layers, geogrids enhance the overall structural capacity and help to reduce surface deformation [ 10 ]. Geogrids have the potential to perform a stabilisation function, making the geogrid-soil composite material less deformable. This effect is due to the interlocking between the geogrid and the soil particles located within its apertures [ 3 ] and contributes to the reduction of the base layer height. In addition, lower costs and emissions associated with the reduction of materials used in construction are other advantages of the use of this type of reinforcement [ 11 ].

Another possibility to purposely reduce the quantity of good-quality materials, lies in the use of wastes and byproducts as partial or total replacement of virgin, natural materials, allowing to reduce the costs of construction [ 12 ]. Several wastes and byproducts generated across different industries have shown potential for incorporation in pavement structures. Road construction considering these materials prevents landfill disposal, and reduces the reliability on natural resources, while still ensuring the required performance [ 13 ]. Magalhães et al. [ 14 ] presented a study on the performance of two steel-slag byproducts mixed with a local clayey soil for use in the base layers of unpaved roads. An experimental road section was built using those mixtures and the results obtained indicated that the gradation and strength of the samples were adequate for use in base layers. Also, pulp and paper industry byproducts have been used in the construction of unpaved roads. Russel [ 15 ] reviewed a range of wood-derived products and byproducts, performing a qualitative assessment of their potential to stabilise low-volume roads constructed on unstable sandy soils. The study revealed that paper mill boiler ash shows significant potential as a recycled material for road stabilization. Elliott et al. [ 16 ] presented a review of proposed and implemented applications of both fly ash and bottom ash from pulp and paper mills using biomass boilers worldwide, highlighting their use in unpaved forest road construction as one example. In Scandinavian countries the biomass boiler ashes are often used for road construction as a stabilizer [ 16 ]. In Sweden, 79% of biomass combustion residues are reused [ 17 ], largely applied in forest road construction. According to Vanhanen et al. [ 18 ], Finland prepares 4000 km annually, and conditions of increasing rainfall and maintenance demands further enhance the feasibility of using ash as a sustainable substitute for natural aggregates in unpaved roads.

An unpaved road is often formed by a good-quality base layer constructed on top on the existing soil (foundation layer or subgrade). Three complementary design approaches are possible [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]: empirical methods that relate observed performance to simple indices and traffic; mechanistic methods that compute stresses, strains, and deflections in layered systems; and mechanistic–empirical approaches that calibrate mechanistic responses to field rutting and deformation under repeated loads. Because of the typically low investments in unpaved forest roads, usually their design relies mostly on semi-empirical, design methods; their output is the base layer height. Among existing methods for unpaved roads, most consider the California Bearing Ratio ( CBR ) value of the foundation layer as the key design parameter [ 22 ,  23 – 24 ]. Other methods, such as Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ], also use the  CBR  value of the base layer. The method proposed by Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ] allows the design of unpaved roads for both unreinforced or reinforced solutions, with geogrids or geotextiles.

Although the  CBR  is not a fundamental material property, its simplicity, low cost, and widespread availability have contributed to its continued use in geotechnical and pavement engineering. Often empirical correlations are used to estimate shear strength parameter and the resilient modulus of soils, linking index testing to fundamental shear strength parameters [ 25 ]. Such correlations are often limited to specific soils and locations and should be used with caution,

Thus, input values of key design properties are critical in design. Soils and aggregates, as well as wastes and byproducts, exhibit variability of properties and characteristics [ 26 ,  27 ]. To allow for such variability in the design and to understand their impact on the design, statistical analysis can be implemented. Such approach has been used in engineering to validate experimental results, optimise processes and compare alternatives and hypotheses [ 28 ]. Visser et al. [ 4 ] uses a parametric statistical method (ANOVA) to determine whether there were significant differences in road strength between treatments and across test periods.

This paper is novel as it includes an integrated approach to the use of industrial residues in unpaved forest roads. The integrated approach includes the characterization of the residues, the design of alternative solutions for an unpaved forest road section, a comparison of associated costs. The main goal is to contribute to promoting a circular economy approach in geotechnics and the adoption of sustainable solutions, while meeting necessary technical requirements. For that, two exhausted sands and their application in the construction of unpaved forest roads, without and with geogrid, were studied and compared to a traditional solution (aggregate also without and with geogrid). The work developed included: (i) geotechnical characterisation of the exhausted sands, including their shear strength and load-bearing response; (ii) statistical analysis to validate  CBR  test results; (iii) design of an unpaved forest road section for different foundation scenarios and considering different solutions for the base layer using unbound materials, traditional solution (aggregate) and solutions using these exhausted sands, without and with geogrid reinforcement; (iv) cost analysis of the solutions obtained for a particular case study.

sections.heading: Approach
paragraphs: The work presented is included in a research project focusing on pulp and paper industry wastes and byproducts and their application on unpaved forest roads. These roads are often designed using simple, empirical methods, based on the California Bearing Ratio ( CBR ) value of the materials selected. Thus, the design of an unpaved forest road section was carried out using such a method, for three different foundation conditions. The solutions studied for the road base layer included: traditional solution (aggregate); exhausted sand; aggregate reinforced with geogrid; and exhausted sand reinforced with geogrid. Finally, a case study was selected for a cost analysis of the solutions designed, varying the base layer material, the strength of the foundation layer, and using geogrid reinforcement.

sections.heading: Exhausted Sands
paragraphs: The two materials studied (Fig.  1 ) are obtained from different biomass boilers that integrate a pulp and paper production process (kraft process, explained by Vilarinho et al. [ 29 ]). Both boilers have a fluidised bed technology and the main difference between these two materials arises from the different materials burned in those boilers. Exhausted sand 1 (ES1) is originated on a calibrated sand (fluidised bed) and the incineration waste from eucalyptus barks. Exhausted sand 2 (ES2) is generated from the same calibrated sand (fluidised bed) and incineration of a variety of forest residues, such as forest biomass, garden waste, and wood industry waste.
Fig. 1 Exhausted sands obtained from biomass boilers analysed:  a ) ES1;  b ) ES2

sections.heading: Identification and Physical Characteristics
paragraphs: The particle density was determined using the pycnometer method described in EN ISO 17892-3 [ 31 ]. The activity of fines was assessed of both exhausted sands using the methylene blue (MB) test, EN ISO 933-9 [ 32 ].
The exhausted sands were classified using the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) by ASTM D2487-11 [ 33 ] and the classification proposed by LCPC/SETRA [ 34 ].

The compaction properties, optimum water content ( w opt ) and maximum dry density ( ρ d, max ), were determined with modified Proctor tests using method C of ASTM D1557-07 [ 35 ]. The internal dimensions of the mould used for this test were: 152.4 ± 0.7 mm in diameter and 116.4 ± 0.5 mm in height. The tests were performed considering only particles of the exhausted sands smaller than 19 mm, and a mechanical rammer that applies a compaction energy of 2700 kN·m/m 3 , as required by the test standard.

sections.heading: Shear Strength of the Exhausted Sands
paragraphs: To assess the shear strength of the exhausted sands, direct shear tests were carried out according to EN ISO 17892-10 [ 36 ]. To ensure representability of the response, particle sizes must be less than 1/6 of the height of the test box. Thus, the test box used (with internal dimensions 60 × 60 × 25 mm 3 ) restrained the particle size inside the box to 4 mm. The tests were carried out at a displacement rate of 1.0 mm/min and the normal stress applied was 50 kPa, 100 kPa and 150 kPa. The samples that were tested under dry conditions.

The test results were used to estimate shear strength parameters for ES1 and ES2, namely the effective angle of friction ( φ′ ). Herein, the case with no effective cohesion was assumed ( c′  = 0 kPa). The strength parameters were obtained for the peak strain and for large deformations (20% of shear strain).

sections.heading: CBR  of the Exhausted Sands
paragraphs: According to the standard ASTM D1883-07 ε2  [ 37 ], the  CBR  value was estimated for two different penetrations, 2.54 mm and 5.08 mm. The  CBR  value is usually taken at a penetration of 2.54 mm. However, if the value at 5.08 mm penetration is higher, the test must be repeated to confirm the result. The standard states that if the  CBR  at 5.08 mm obtained in the repeat test is still higher this should be taken as the most representative. However, in this study, the results of both penetrations were analysed.

The test method does not prescribe a minimum number of test specimens. Thus, often the  CBR  of an unbound material is estimated from the results of a single specimen. Due to the inherent variability of unbound materials this is likely to be a limitation. Herein, three specimens per condition were studied, to ensure some statistical representativity.

sections.heading: Statistical Analysis of the  CBR  Test Results
paragraphs: A statistical analysis of the  CBR  test results was carried out. This was complemented with plotting stress-strain curves for the different materials and their respective confidence intervals. The statistical analysis used the IBM SPSS 30.0 (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) software.

To define the type of method applicable for the statistical analysis, the data distribution type and the homogeneity of variances were assessed. Thus, parametric or non-parametric methods were used to analyse the hypothesis. The null hypothesis ( H 0 ) of this study is that there are no significant differences between the  CBR  values of ES1 and ES2; the alternative hypothesis ( H 1 ) is that are significant differences between those  CBR  values. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to determine the type of data distribution, considering that the number of samples was small (3  per  condition); the Levene’s test was used to determine the homogeneity of variances. A confidence interval ( CI ) of 95% and a significance level of 5% were assumed. The p-value is used to assess the statistical significance of the results obtained. A significance level ( α ) of 0.05 (5%) was used as the criterion value to reject the null hypothesis. The p-value indicates the possibility of reaching a result as extreme as the one observed, assuming the authenticity of the null hypothesis. If the p-value is greater than the significance level (p-value >  α ), the null hypothesis is not rejected, and vice versa.

sections.heading: Unpaved Road Design Method
paragraphs: Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ] pointed out some limitations of the method: the rut depth range is limited (50 mm to 100 mm); the  CBR  value of the foundation layer has an upper limit (< 5%); the method only allows  J  < 0.80 N·m/º.

The fixed input values used in this study for the design method Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ] are shown in Table  1 . Each solution for the base layer was represented by its corresponding average  CBR  value.

sections.heading: Aim and Solutions Analysed
paragraphs: A case study was defined to allow direct comparison of solutions for an unpaved forest road section, including a cost analysis. The solutions studied included different unbound materials for the base layer: exhausted sand 1 (ES1); exhausted sand 2 (ES2); a good-quality aggregate (AG). Additional solutions included the same unbound materials for the base layer with a geogrid at the bottom of that layer. Two different geogrids were studied (GG1 and GG2). In total, 9 different solutions were analysed: ES1, ES2, AG, ES1+GG1, ES2+GG1, AG+GG1, ES1+GG2, ES2+GG2, and AG+GG2.

Based on the geotechnical properties obtained using laboratory tests and some data from the literature, each of these 9 solutions was designed. That entailed defining the base layer height using the Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ] method (Sect. 2.7) and rounding it up to the nearest 0.05 m.

Then, a cost analysis was carried out. The main goal was to assess if there are relevant cost differences between solutions using a traditional material (such as a good quality aggregate) and the selected exhausted sands, without or with geogrid reinforcement. A simplified approach was adopted, with only acquisition and transport costs of materials to the construction site assumed as varying.

sections.heading: Additional Material Properties
paragraphs: For the design and subsequent cost analyses, additional materials and their properties were defined. The materials used were extruded polypropylene biaxial geogrids, designated as GG1 and GG2. GG1 features a tensile strength of 20.0 kN/m, a 38 × 38 mm mesh opening size, and an aperture stability value of  J  = 0.48 N·m/º. Meanwhile, GG2 exhibits a higher tensile strength of 30.0 kN/m, the same 38 × 38 mm mesh opening size, and an aperture stability value of  J  = 0.80 N·m/º.According to Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ], this parameter influences the stress distribution angle within the base layer and, thus, affects the ability of the base layer to distribute normal stresses. Additionally, the aggregate (AG) was considered an unbound, well graded aggregate, typically used for unpaved forest road construction; its  CBR  value was assumed to be 80% [ 39 ].

sections.heading: Assumptions Made for the Cost Analysis
paragraphs: The sources or providers of the materials necessary for the 9 solutions analysed needed to be defined, for the case study analysed: ES1 and ES2 originated from the pulp and paper mill (where the biomass boilers are); aggregate AG was extracted from a quarry; geogrids GG1 and GG2 were obtained from their supplier (in Portugal). The distance from each of these three locations to the construction site defined for the case study was assumed fixed and to be the same: 100 km (Fig.  2 ).
Fig. 2 Case study distances relative to the road construction site (1) from: Exhausted sand generation factory (2); Geogrid supplier (3); Quarry (4)

For the cost analysis, it was assumed that the road construction process was the same for all 9 solutions studied. The cost associated to the site installation of the reinforcement (GG1 or GG2) was considered negligible, as it only required residual labour and resources already available on site. Therefore, the cost analysis only accounted for acquisition and transport process of all materials to the construction site, representing a simplified approach.

An unpaved forest road section with 1000 m length and 6 m width was analysed. The foundation conditions analysed were varied and corresponded to 3 different  CBR  values (1%, 3%, and 4.99%), within the limits allowed by the design method used.

The unitary costs considered are shown in Table  2 . The acquisition costs for the aggregate and reinforcements were obtained through their potential suppliers; no commercial value was assigned to the exhausted sands studied. Similarly, the transport costs for the materials (AG, ES1 and ES2) were obtained through suppliers, considering a semi-trailer with maximum capacity of 22 t, assumed to operate at full capacity. The reinforcement transport costs were obtained using an open access transportation cost calculation tool [ 40 ] for a 7.5 t truck; for these costs, a constant rate for distances up to 65 km and a variable cost function beyond that range (equation in Table  1 ) were assumed.

Table 2 Unitary costs used in the case study Activity Cost Acquisition Exhausted sand 1 and 2 (ES1 and ES2) 0.00 €/t Aggregate (AG) 6.75 €/t Geogrid 1 (GG1) 1.04 €/m 2 Geogrid 2 (GG2) 1.59 €/m 2 Transport Aggregate and Exhausted sands (AG, ES1 and ES2) 0.12 €/(t·km) Geogrids (GG1 and GG2) for distance D in km 0 to 65 km 75 € > 65 km 75 + 0.80 × (D – 65) €
At a final stage, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the influence on the results of the transport distance between the exhausted sand origin and the construction site.

sections.heading: Identification and Physical Characteristics
paragraphs: Figure  3  includes the particle size distribution of the two exhausted sands studied, ES1 and ES2, which was obtained according to the standard EN ISO 933-1 [ 30 ] (sieving method). This figure also includes the particle size distribution of the portions of materials used to perform the  CBR  tests (ES2 < 19 mm) and direct shear tests (ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm), after removing particles larger than 19 mm and 4 mm, respectively. These curves were mathematically derived from the original curves of the materials. ES1 and ES1 < 4 mm were quite similar materials; the differences observed could be due to inherent variability of a soil. The same observation is valid for ES2 and ES2 < 19 mm; while ES2 < 4 mm was much finer than ES2. Table  3  summarises the effective diameters, and  C U  and  C C  for these different materials. For ES1 and ES1 < 4 mm these parameters practically coincided, illustrating the similarity between these materials. Removing particles larger than 19 mm or 4 mm of ES2 led to reductions in effective diameters and  C U  and increased the percentage of fine particles. Comparing the particle sizes distribution of the materials tested in direct shear, ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm, the latter was still coarser than ES1 < 4 mm, showing that the particles of sand of ES2 were larger.
Fig. 3 Particle size distribution of the exhausted sands studied and for the same materials without particles larger than 4 mm and 19 mm:  a ) ES1;  b ) ES2

The particle density (assessed using EN ISO 17892-3 [ 31 ], pycnometer method) and the particle unit weight obtained for ES1 and ES2 were very similar, ~ 2.64 g/cm 3 , within the typical range for natural geotechnical materials ( ρ s  = 2.638 g/cm 3 , ES1;  ρ s  = 2.647 g/cm 3 , ES2). The fine particles of both ES1 and ES2 were not sensitive to water, as the methylene blue (MB) values obtained using EN ISO 933-9 Methylene Blue test [ 32 ], were 0.25 g/kg, significantly lower than the reference limit of 1.0 g/kg (LCPC/SETRA [ 34 ]). Some of these results have been presented by Martins et al. (2024) [ 41 ]. The Proctor compaction tests were conducted according to the standard ASTM D1557-07 [ 35 ] and their results are summarised in Fig.  4 . From the results it was possible to define the optimum water content,  w opt , and the corresponding maximum dry density values of 10.8% and 1671 kg.m − 3  for ES1, and 11.0% and 1781 kg/m 3  for ES2 < 19 mm, respectively.
Fig. 4 Relation between degree of saturation, specific volume, dry density, and water content obtained in the modified Proctor tests of the exhausted sands studied:  a ) ES1;  b ) ES2 < 19 mm

Considering the characterisation tests and the classifications adopted herein, USCS by ASTM D2487-11 [ 33 ] and LCPC/SETRA [ 34 ], it was possible to classify ES1 and ES1 < 4 mm as a poorly graded sand (SP) and a clean alluvial sand, dune sands (D 1 ), respectively. Conversely, ES2 was classified as well-graded sand with gravel (SW) and as clean alluvial gravel, sand (D 2 ). However, the sieved fractions of ES2 show poorer gradation: both ES2 < 19 mm and ES2 < 4 mm were classified as poorly graded sand (SP). The ES2 < 19 mm fraction was classified as clean alluvial gravel, sand (D 2 ), while the ES < 4 mm fraction was described identically to ES1 < 4 mm, as clean alluvial sand or dune sands (D 1 ).

sections.heading: Shear Strength of the Exhausted Sands
paragraphs: The strength parameters of the exhausted sands studied were obtained from direct shear tests assuming zero effective cohesion. These exhausted sands presented a low percentage of fine particles (< 3.3%) and low MB values, consistent with those of cohesionless materials.

Figure  5  summarises the direct shear tests results obtained for ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm (obtained from ES1 and ES2, respectively, after removing particles larger than 4 mm). Qualitatively, the relationship between shear stress and shear strain (for different normal stresses) of the two materials were similar (Fig.  5 a and b). The shear stress increased with increasing shear strain until it reached a peak. After the peak, softening was observed. For ES1 < 4 mm there was indication of reaching critical state at the end of test; for ES2 < 4 mm no evidence of critical state was observed. As expected, higher normal stress was associated with higher peak shear stress.

Fig. 5 Results of the direct shear tests: Shear stress vs. shear strain relationship under different normal stresses for  a ) ES1 < 4 mm;  b ) ES2 < 4 mm; Volumetric strain vs shear strain under different normal stresses for  c ) ES1 < 4 mm;  d ) ES2 < 4 mm; Relationship between shear stress and normal stress for  e ) the peak and  f ) 20% shearing strain.

The variation in volumetric strain as a function of shear strain was also qualitatively similar for ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm (Fig.  5 c e Fig.  5 d). Initially, both materials exhibited contraction (more pronounced for ES1 < 4 mm), followed by a dilatant response with increased shear strain. This is typical of dense materials with a peak shear stress.

Figure  5 e and f shows the failure envelopes, for both materials, at peak and for large shear strains, respectively. It can be observed that ES2 < 4 mm had greater shear resistance. The coefficient of determination  R 2  was high, ranging between 0.994 and 0.999, further confirming that the effective cohesion of these materials was zero. The peak angle of friction values obtained were within the typical range for sand and gravel [ 42 ]: 45.4º and 54.5º for ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm, respectively. For large deformations (20% shearing strain), the angle of friction obtained was closer to critical state condition: 37.8° and 45.3°, respectively, for ES1 < 4 mm and ES2 < 4 mm.

sections.heading: CBR  of the Exhausted Sands
paragraphs: Table  4  summarises the  CBR  values for ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm for three tests  per  condition and for two penetration values (2.54 mm and 5.08 mm), the corresponding average, standard deviation and coefficient of variation. For both materials, the highest  CBR  value corresponded to 5.08 mm penetration, which was the  CBR  value considered for each material: 40% for ES1 and 37% for ES2 < 19 mm.

Table 4 CBR  values for 2.54 mm and 5.08 mm penetrations of ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm Test CBR (%) ES1 CBR (%) ES2 < 19 mm 2.54 mm 5.08 mm 2.54 mm 5.08 mm Specimen 1 34.7 42.0 28.6 33.7 Specimen 2 35.6 40.1 30.8 36.8 Specimen 3 32.5 38.2 37.2 41.2 Average 34.3 40.1 32.2 37.2 Standard deviation 1.3 1.6 3.7 3.1 Coefficient of variation 3.8% 4.0% 11.5% 8.3%

The average  CBR  values of ES1 were 34% and 40%, for 2.54 mm and 5.08 mm penetration, respectively; the corresponding scatter of results was small (coefficient of variation of ~ 4%). For ES2 < 19 mm, the average  CBR  values were 32% and 37% for 2.54 mm and 5.08 mm penetration, respectively; nevertheless, the scatter of results observed was larger than for ES1, with coefficients of variation of 12% and 8%, respectively. In addition, for both penetrations, the range of values for ES2 < 19 mm was greater than that for ES1.

sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
paragraphs: The statistical analysis was carried out for the  CBR  values obtained for 5.08 mm penetration. Table  5  shows the result obtained from the Shapiro-Wilk normality test. For the normality test two hypotheses were assumed:  H o , the distribution of the data was normal; and  H 1 , the distribution of the data was non-normal. The p-value obtained was larger than 0.05, indicating that the  CBR  values of each exhausted sand have a normal distribution.

Table 5 Results of the Shapiro-Wilk test for the type of distribution and of the Levene’s test for the homogeneity of variances Parameter Condition Test p -value p -value Conclusion CBR ES1 Shapiro-Wilk 1.00 > 0.05 Normal distribution ES2 < 19 mm 0.81 ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm Levene’s 0.34 > 0.05 Homogeneous variances

The hypotheses assumed for the homogeneity of variances were:  H 0 , the variances of the  CBR  values of the exhausted sands were homogeneous;  H 1 , the variances of the  CBR  values of exhausted sands were not homogeneous. Table  5  shows the results of the Levene’s test to verify the homogeneity of the variances, where a p-value > 0.05 was obtained. This means that the variances were homogeneous. After these verifications, it was then possible to carry out a parametric test, Student’s t-test. This parametric test aims to verify statistical differences between the means of two independent groups. Its requirements are the normality of the data for each group, the independence of the tests and the homogeneity of the variances; in this case, these three conditions were verified.

The p-value obtained from the statistical analysis (with 4 degrees of freedom, a t-test value of 1.18 and an average difference of 2.87) was higher (p-value = 0.31) than the significance level (0.05). It was not possible to reject the null hypothesis ( H 0 ), concluding that there were no statistically significant differences between the  CBR  values of the two exhausted sands.

To better understand the response of ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm during the  CBR  test and analyse if there were differences between them, average stress  versus  normalised penetration curves were plotted, with the respective 95% confidence interval (Fig.  6 ). Penetrations of 2.54 mm and 5.08 mm correspond to normalised penetrations (in relation to the size of the piston) of 5.08% and 10.16%, respectively. For both penetrations the confidence intervals for ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm overlapped, confirming that there were no statistically significant differences between the two exhausted sand. For normalised penetrations larger than ~ 13%, the curves did not overlap anymore, i.e., the stress-penetration relation of ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm became statistically different.
Fig. 6 Average stress values  versus  the normalised penetration curves and corresponding upper and lower 95% confidence intervals for ES1 and ES2 < 19 mm

sections.heading: Design of the Unpaved Forest Road
paragraphs: Table  6  shows the height of the base layer for different solutions, unreinforced and with geogrid reinforcement, obtained from the design method by Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ]. The results were rounded up to multiples of 0.05 m, as such rounded values are adopted in real applications. A minimum height for the base layer was imposed in the design method, considering the rut depth and the radius of equivalent tire contact area; for the cases analysed that minimum height was 0.10 m. All values of 0.10 m in Table  6  refer to such cases, in which the output of the design method was below the minimum height.

Table 6 Base layer height for the 9 solutions studied obtained using the method by Giroud and Han [ 20 ,  21 ] and rounded up to multiples of 0.05 m Solutions Base layer height (m) CBR  FL =1% CBR  FL =3% CBR  FL =4.99% ES1 0.60 0.35 0.30 ES2 0.60 0.40 0.30 AG 0.60 0.35 0.25 ES1 + GG1 0.35 0.10 0.10 ES2 + GG1 0.35 0.10 0.10 AG+GG1 0.35 0.10 0.10 ES1 + GG2 0.10 0.10 0.10 ES2 + GG2 0.10 0.10 0.10 AG+GG2 0.10 0.10 0.10
The solutions analysed are designated ES1 and ES2; nevertheless, the  CBR  value assumed for ES2 was that obtained for ES2 < 19 mm, as discussed previously.

Considering a base layer formed by ES1 or ES2 (unreinforced), the different foundation conditions analysed did not change the height of the base layer, except for  CBR FL  = 3% (the height of ES2 was 14.3% larger than that of ES1). This is explained by the differences in  CBR  values, as the  CBR  value of ES2 was lower than that of ES1. Although the statistical analysis carried out showed that the  CBR  values obtained for these two materials were not statistically different, average  CBR  values were used as input for the design method. Using the exhausted sands ES1 or ES2 instead of the traditional aggregate, AG, did not change the base layer height for the weaker foundation condition analysed ( CBR FL  = 1%). For  CBR FL  = 4.99%, the height of AG was ~ 17% smaller than that of ES1 and ES2, mostly due to the higher  CBR  value of AG.

The benefit of including a geogrid layer at the interface between the foundation and the base layer was evident from the results, as the height of the base layer was significantly reduced when GG1 or GG2 were considered. Thus, the quantity of unbound materials and associated resources needed for the reinforced solutions also decreased relatively to the unreinforced ones. For most cases analysed which included a geogrid reinforcement, the height of the base layer corresponded to the minimum height prescribed in the design method (0.10 m). The exceptions found refer to the weaker foundation condition ( CBR FL = 1%) and the lower  J  value (GG1).

As mentioned before, this minimum base layer height results directly from the design method. Nevertheless, it must be pointed out that this height may need to be increased, to ensure the geogrid survives the site installation processes. Such analysis was not considered herein.

sections.heading: Summary of Results
paragraphs: The costs analysis was carried out for an unpaved forest road with 1000 m length and 6 m width (as described in Sect. Assumptions made for the cost analysis). In the analysis three factors were studied: the type of material adopted for the base layer (ES1, ES2, and AG); the  CBR  of the foundation layer (1%, 3%, and 4.99%); the use of a reinforcement layer (without reinforcement, with GG1, and with GG2). From the height of the base layer obtained from the design (Sect. Design of the unpaved forest road), the volume of materials needed was calculated. This allowed predicting transport conditions (number of trips necessary to transport the volumes needed) and acquisition costs of each material. The global cost of each solution was compiled in Fig.  7 .

Fig. 7 Cost estimates in €/m 2  for the different solutions for the base layer and considering:  a ) foundation layer  CBR  of 1%;  b ) foundation layer  CBR  of 3%;  c ) foundation layer  CBR  of 4.99%

The distribution of costs through the different activities (acquisition and transport) depended on the material analysed: ES1, ES2, and AG; and GG1 and GG2. Transport of materials that constitute the base layer had greater cost impact, relative to their acquisition. For example, in solutions considering AG and the weakest foundation condition ( CBR FL  = 1%), transport costs represented 64% of the total cost. For the reinforced solutions, the quantity of aggregate needed was reduced and acquisition and transport costs for the geogrid reinforcement considered were added. However, the transport cost of AG still contributed the most for the overall costs: 60% and 47%, when considering GG1 and GG2, respectively. The geogrid contributions to the overall cost, especially their transport, were insignificant compared to operations related to the base layer materials.

sections.heading: Influence of the Material Adopted for the Base Layer
paragraphs: The material adopted for the base layer is a key variable in this analysis. The aggregate, AG, a good-quality material ( CBR  of 80%), had geotechnical properties and costs different from those of the exhausted sands. Given the zero cost of acquisition for the exhausted sands, all solutions with ES1 or ES2 come at lower cost in comparison with AG, with and without reinforcement (Fig.  7 ). This showed that, despite the decrease in  CBR  value, there were still cost benefits when using exhausted sands relative to AG. There was a small difference in costs for ES1 and ES2, related to the maximum dry density value of these exhausted sands. This led to higher acquisition and transport costs for solutions with ES2. However, when making a cost analysis, both materials were still better than AG.

sections.heading: Influence of the Foundation Layer (CBR FL )
paragraphs: The  CBR  value of the foundation layer directly affects the cost estimates for each solution. Weaker foundation layers led to lager height for the base layer, to ensure adequate support capacity. While for foundations with  CBR  of 1% the costs came up to 25.90 €/m 2  for AG, with the increase in foundation capacity this cost was reduced 42% (-10.79 €/m 2 ) and 58% (-15.11 €/m 2 ), for  CBR FL  of 3% and 4.99%, respectively.

In summary, as the capacity of foundation layer rose, the volume of materials needed to obtain the desired conditions reduced, therefore, reducing the cost of the solution. The  CBR  value of the foundation layer also influenced the choice of reinforcement, as shown in the next section.

sections.heading: Influence of the Reinforcement
paragraphs: The inclusion of a geogrid between the foundation and the base layers led to a reduction of construction costs of the unpaved forest road analysed. This was a direct consequence of the smaller height for the base layer obtained from the design method and, thus, of smaller quantities of unbound materials needed than for unreinforced solutions. Consequently, there was a clear reduction of both acquisition and transport costs associated with the materials needed, even with the additional cost of acquisition and transport of the geogrid adopted in each case. For example, the results showed that the transport of the geogrid was considered irrelevant for the overall cost (less than 1%).

The acquisition costs of GG2 (1.59 €/m 2 ) were higher than those of GG1 (1.04 €/m 2 ), given their different physical and mechanical properties, including their aperture stability ( J ). However, the results showed that GG2, with better mechanical properties, was not always the most efficient in terms of cost. Regardless of the foundation conditions, the acquisition of the reinforcement had greater impacts for solutions with GG2 than with GG1 (Fig.  7 ).

For the weakest foundation conditions analysed ( CBR FL  = 1%), despite being the more expensive, GG2 had a more effective reduction of the base layer height (~ 70 to ~ 80%) relative that GG1 (~ 30 to ~ 40%). For all the base layer materials studied, including a reinforcement reduced the height of the base layer from 0.60 m (unreinforced) to 0.35 m (GG1) or to 0.10 m (GG2). Thus, when analysing costs, GG2 was better, as its higher cost was compensated for by the significant decrease in volumes of material needed.

For  CBR FL  of 3% and 4.99%, both geogrids led to the minimum height of the base layer (0.10 m). Therefore, for these conditions, solutions incorporating GG1 were the most cost-efficient than with GG2, as they required the same volume of material, while using a more affordable geogrid, for the same requirements.

sections.heading: Sensitivity Analysis
paragraphs: The case study analysed included fixed distances; this overlooks the potential impact of the location of exhausted sands supplier on the results. Therefore, while maintaining all other distances at 100 km, the transport distance of the exhausted sands was varied, and two alternative scenarios were analysed: 50 km (a potentially close location) and 150 km (distant scenario). The results showed, in Fig.  7 , that in both scenarios the cost of solutions with ES1 and ES2 were still better than solutions using AG.

To further assess the benefit of considering these exhausted sands, for each foundation condition considered ( CBR  of 1%, 3% and 4.99%) another analysis was carried out. The goal was to determine the distance beyond which the transport cost of the exhausted sands outweighed their economic benefit, compared to AG. These results are summarised in Fig.  8 . For example, when the transport distance of ES1 exceeded 214.8 km, the solution with 0.60 m base layer of AG became more cost-effective than the one using 0.60 m base layer of ES1. This indicates that, despite ES1 having no acquisition cost, there was a threshold beyond which it was no longer the most cost-effective solution, associated with the transport distances.
Fig. 8 Distances from the exhausted sands origin to the construction site (in km) below which the use of exhausted sands is still beneficial in relation to the AG

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Research Needs
paragraphs: Using alternative materials, such as the exhausted sands studied, may cause additional challenges, namely environmental. Herein, the chemical properties and contamination potential of the exhausted sands were not evaluated. To make a confident selection of materials, factors such as leachability must be assessed. Nevertheless, technical guidelines for the use of construction and demolition wastes [ 43 ] prescribe that such materials can be used in geotechnical applications, provided that all necessary requirements regarding their contamination potential are met. This is done by ensuring that the construction and demolition wastes comply with legal limits for their disposal in inert waste landfills, as defined in Decree-Law nº 152/2002 of May 23nd [ 44 ]. Such approach can be extended to other residues, as the exhausted sands studied herein. According to the European Union (EU) list of wastes [ 45 ], ashes from fluidized-bed boilers, particularly those used for power generation, as is the case of the exhausted sands studied in this paper, are always classified as non-hazardous waste. Thus, it is key that in the future a detailed and comprehensive characterisation of these exhausted sands is carried out, to check if they fully meet the legal limits for disposal as inert waste, as prescribed by EU directives.

The  CBR  test is widely used in pavement design and geotechnical engineering due to its simplicity; however, it has several limitations [ 46 ]. Unbound coarse material and soils are, by nature, heterogeneous materials and their  CBR  value depends on characteristics of the granular matrix, such as its dry density (compaction conditions), saturation, composition, and water content.  CBR  values are highly sensitive to the water content, and small variations can affect significantly the results obtained. This is particularly relevant in the field, where moisture conditions can vary significantly. All the tests carried out in the present study were carried out without immersing the test specimens, which are an unconservative approximation of  CBR  values after immersion. The difference of  CBR  values with and without immersion is more important for materials with higher proportion of fine particles and their sensitivity to water.

CBR  results should always be interpreted together with compaction and moisture conditions, for example, rather than as an isolated material property. This heterogeneity justifies the use of more than one specimen to have a more representative value of the  CBR . However, the test method does not prescribe a minimum number of test specimens. Thus, in practice the  CBR  of an unbound material is often estimated from the results of a single specimen. Herein, three specimens per condition were tested to increase representativity, although it is still relatively small number considering the inherent variability of granular materials.

Another limitation of the  CBR  tests is their scale, as the test mould (152 mm diameter, 125 mm height) and plunger (50 mm diameter) used were small relatively to the maximum particle size of ES2. The test method tries to overcome such limitations by prescribing the removal of particles larger than 19 mm. This procedure may lead to deviations of the measured  CBR  value (in laboratory) from the “true”  CBR  value of the unbound material studied. In addition, the volume of soil mobilised in the  CBR  test is small and may not be representative of its field response.

Sustainability in unpaved roads involves the development and maintenance of road infrastructure that meets transportation needs while minimizing environmental impacts. The use of alternative solutions, such as residues from different industries, combined with geosynthetics, is a possible path to reach that goal. However, this requires addressing different perspectives to ensure that environmental, economic, and social considerations are considered. After ensuring the technical feasibility of the solutions, it is essential to carry out detailed studies to quantify costs and environmental impacts. In this work, a simplified cost analysis is presented, which shows some of the economic benefits of combining exhausted sands and geogrids. Recent studies have corroborated these findings, showing that, from both an economic and an environmental perspective, these solutions can generate financial savings and reduce environmental impacts, particularly in terms of pollutant emissions [ 47 ,  48 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This paper assessed the benefits of combining exhausted sands and the construction of unpaved forest roads, enhanced with a geogrid. The work included: geotechnical characterisation of two exhausted sands, their shear strength and load-bearing response ( CBR  tests); design of an unpaved forest road section for different foundation scenarios and considering different solutions for the base layer; cost analysis of the solutions designed for a particular case study. For the base layer, different unbound coarse materials were analysed, traditional solution (aggregate) and each of the two exhausted sands (ES1 and ES2), without and with geogrid reinforcement. The case study only considered acquisition and transport of materials into a construction site. The results showed that:

The exhausted sands studied were similar to unbound granular materials, corresponding to a poorly graded sand (ES1) and a well-graded sand with gravel (ES2). Three specimens per condition were submitted to  CBR  tests and the statistical analysis carried out (Student’s t-test) showed that there were no statistically significant differences between the  CBR  values of the two exhausted sands. Their stress-penetration curves (from  CBR  tests) overlapped for normalised penetrations lower than ~ 13%, while for higher penetration values the responses became statistically different. The empirical design of the base layer was highly dependent on the  CBR  value of the material chosen for that layer. As there were no statistical differences for the two exhausted sands studied, no relevant differences emerged. As expected, the stronger the base layer material and the foundation conditions, the smaller the required base layer height. A geogrid layer placed at the interface between the foundation and the base layer overcomes potential reductions of  CBR  when using exhausted sands, leading to important decreases of the height of the base layer. Relatively to the cost and for the case study analysed, adopting a base layer formed by one of the exhausted sands studied had economic benefits relative to a traditional, good-quality aggregate. This was further enhanced when a geogrid was included, due to the associated reduction in volumes of materials needed. The proportion of the benefit depended on both the aperture modulus of the geogrid and on the  CBR  of the foundation layer.

The combined use of geogrid reinforcement and residues as alternatives to good-quality aggregates in unpaved roads can enhance bearing capacity, reduce rutting, improve trafficability, and decrease aggregate consumption. This approach promotes the beneficial reuse of non-conventional materials while increasing the structural efficiency of these infrastructures. Consequently, it offers a promising strategy for developing more sustainable and cost-effective unpaved road infrastructure, particularly in regions where high-quality construction materials are scarce or expensive. In short, the results obtained suggest that using these exhausted sands promotes sustainability and circular economy.
